links.note: Richard Allen tells how white Methodist elders fought Bethel church in Philadelphia for its pulpit. One elder published a letter that disowned its members, and a lawsuit followed that Bethel won. In April 1816 Black Methodists from Philadelphia and Baltimore formed the African Methodist Episcopal Church.

sources.work: Richard Allen, The Life, Experience, and Gospel Labors of the Rt. Rev. Richard Allen (1880 reprint of 1833)

prose_changes.old: Child of Methodist/Edwardsean lines; parent of Restorationist and Holiness traditions
prose_changes.new: Grew out of frontier revivals that Methodist preachers helped to run. The Stone-Campbell Restoration movement came out of it, and the later Holiness movement took up its camp meeting.
prose_changes.reason: 'Edwardsean lines' removed: no vendored text shows the frontier revival using Edwards (Finney's Lectures, not vendored, would test it; in wants). 'Parent of Holiness' qualified to the camp meeting the Holiness movement took up, since Holiness's own text puts its start in Methodist teaching. Short code-style summary rewritten as plain sentences.

prose_changes.old: At Cane Ridge in August 1801, crowds estimated as high as twenty thousand camped in the woods for a week of preaching, weeping, and shouting. Methodist circuit riders and Baptist preachers carried that pattern across the frontier, and by the 1830s Charles Finney was teaching revival as a method that could be worked deliberately rather than simply awaited. Two later movements, the Stone-Campbell Restoration and the Holiness movement, grew directly out of this ferment.
prose_changes.new: At Cane Ridge in August 1801, crowds estimated as high as twenty thousand camped in the woods for a week of preaching, weeping, and shouting. Methodist circuit riders and Baptist preachers carried that pattern across the frontier, and by the 1830s Charles Finney was teaching revival as a method that could be worked deliberately rather than simply awaited. The Stone-Campbell Restoration movement grew directly out of this ferment, and the later Holiness movement took up its camp meeting.
prose_changes.reason: 'The Holiness movement grew directly out of this ferment' overstates the evidence: Holiness grew from Methodist teaching in the 1830s and later took up the camp meeting. Stone-Campbell claim kept; it is documented by McNemar.

prose_changes.old: It made revivalism a permanent feature of American religion rather than an occasional event, and handed on a whole toolkit still in use — the protracted meeting, the altar call, the anxious bench, the campground and its choruses. Two traditions came directly out of its ferment: the Stone-Campbell Restoration movement and, by way of Methodism's perfectionist wing, the Holiness movement and eventually Pentecostalism. Its campgrounds outlived the frontier, turning into summer resorts, Chautauqua assemblies and conference centers that are still in use.
prose_changes.new: It made revivalism a permanent feature of American religion rather than an occasional event, and handed on a whole toolkit still in use — the protracted meeting, the altar call, the anxious bench, the campground and its choruses. The Stone-Campbell Restoration movement came directly out of its ferment. The Holiness movement, which grew from Methodist teaching, later held camp meetings of its own, and Pentecostalism grew in turn from Holiness. Many of its campgrounds outlived the frontier.
prose_changes.reason: Holiness descent qualified to match the evidence (Methodist origin, camp meeting taken up). The campgrounds-into-Chautauqua claim removed: no vendored or repo-cited source supports it; the plain fact that campgrounds outlasted the frontier is kept.
